en: Let's start with the linear search
algorithm. It's the easiest search
algorithm, which does not mean that it's a
bad algorithm.
Let's consider an array of data that looks
like that. And again, it wouldn't have to be
numbers, but that's easiest and therefore
makes understanding this algorithm easier.
Now let's say we're looking for the number
5. The linear search algorithm is a very
simple algorithm.
The linear search algorithm does what you
probably would do as well if you're
confronted with the task of finding the
element with the value 5 in this array.
You would probably have a look at every
element in the array, and the first time you
see 5, you stop and you return that value
and/or the index of that value.
And that's exactly what the linear search
algorithm does. It goes through this
through this list of data step by step from
the beginning to the end, and it stops once
it finds the value it's looking for, and
then it returns that value or the index of
that value, whatever you wanna have.
So linear search is really simple and it
works on ordered and unordered lists. So the
list doesn't have to be sorted because
you're simply having a look at all items
until you find the element for the first
time anyways. And that's important. If you
have the same element twice in that list, in
this array, you would simply stop the first
time you find it. That's the idea behind
such search algorithms. You return the first
found element.
Now that's linear search. Let's write such
an algorithm and let's thereafter judge the
time complexity.
